top.line: Open source is paid for, often only in time
top.para: An old Intel iMac that could not run Homebrew or Docker Desktop shows why projects drop old machines: support costs money and the long tail cannot easily pay. Simulated, about £1.80 a machine a year from individuals covers one project's long-tail cost in half the draws; customised company builds cover it in 94%.

s0.line: The long tail is large, and companies pay reliably
s0.para: Homebrew shows 16.66% of yearly macOS installs on versions older than the newest three, and 18.55% of pip downloads run end-of-life Python. Oracle earned $19.8 billion from support, while open source gets about 0.09% of its value. Micro-payments roughly cover the long tail; customised builds cover it in 94% of draws.

imac.line: The iMac story was mostly right, a little unfair
imac.para: A clean macOS 13 Ventura install, unpatched since 13.7.8 in August 2025, could not run Homebrew, which now refuses all Intel Macs, or Docker Desktop, which needs macOS 14. Python came from python.org and MacPorts still works. Every project dropped the machine because support costs CI hardware and maintainer time nobody pays for.

measured.line: Millions of installs still come from old macOS versions
measured.para: Homebrew's analytics show 6.99% of install events over 30 days and 16.66% over a year from versions older than the newest three, with 4.64 million yearly from Ventura and 4.94 million from Monterey. On PyPI, 18.55% of pip downloads use end-of-life Python, and Black Duck found four-year-old components in 92% of codebases.

money.line: Old versions earn billions when vendors own the code
money.para: Open source is valued at $8.8 trillion but receives about $7.7 billion a year, roughly 0.09%, and 60% of maintainers are unpaid hobbyists. Meanwhile Oracle earned $19.8 billion from support, Red Hat ran subscriptions at about 93% margin, and Rimini Street earned about $136,000 per client. Community code gets a donation jar.

charge.line: Charging works, but forks, bans and gaming follow
charge.para: Docker Desktop's 2021 licence passed $50 million in recurring revenue, yet alternatives now make up about 47% of container-tool installs in Homebrew. HashiCorp, Elastic and Redis relicensing produced well-funded forks. Open core weakens the free version, and tea.xyz's per-install rewards brought spam, so payment must be tied to verified users.

pence.line: Card fees make pence payments viable only aggregated
pence.para: Stripe's UK rate of 1.5% plus 20p is 2.5% of £20, 5.5% of £5 and 41.5% of 50p, so below about £5 the fixed fee is the price. Pence only work as one annual charge across many projects or a platform settling in bulk, which this site's reading meter now tests.

models.line: Donations fail the long tail; company builds cover it
models.para: A Monte Carlo model of one Homebrew-scale project, with a long-tail cost of about £27,000 a year, ran 10,000 draws through five payment models. Donations cover the cost in 24% of draws, age-rising support 54%, micro-paid builds about 60%, customised company builds 94%, and a seat licence 99.9%, though only if spent on old platforms.

break-even.line: About £2 a machine yearly covers the tail, usually
break-even.para: With typical conversion, supported builds cover the long-tail cost in half the draws at £1.80 aggregated or £1.90 by card, and at 70p with great conversion. No price reaches nine in ten, because raising the price loses more payers than it gains, and with pessimistic conversion no price works at all.

sensitivity.line: Installed base size matters more than whether people pay
sensitivity.para: The assumptions that move the result most are install events per machine, a swing of about £90,000 in the median margin, then willingness to pay, about £47,000, and the long-tail share, about £43,000. Conversion matters less than expected, and two of these could be measured by a project selling supported builds.

satellites.line: Company money could sustain about 18 small support firms
satellites.para: Assuming firms of two or three engineers costing about £240,000 a year and supporting ten projects each, the model sustains a median of about 18 firms worldwide, about one per country, mostly from company builds. Rimini Street, at about $136,000 per client, proves a satellite market forms where money flows.

says.line: Sell supported builds, not donations or weaker free versions
says.para: Individuals paying about £2 a machine a year can roughly cover the long tail, but companies buying customised builds below their own cost are the reliable money, as at RiskMandate and sgit. What is missing is plumbing: one annual charge across projects, payment tied to verified builds, and a split with local support firms.

check.line: Every number and assumption is open to check
check.para: The Long Tail Ledger vault holds 175 sourced facts, 26 case facts and 36 assumptions with ranges, the Python model and a browser calculator with sliders, matched exactly on 77 input grids. The model forecasts no revenue, and the claim about Docker Desktop bans is not supported by any survey found.

sources.line: Sources: vendor docs, filings, surveys and earlier positions
sources.para: The iMac case was checked against Apple, Homebrew, Docker, Python, MacPorts and OpenCore Legacy Patcher documentation on 10 October 2026. The economics draw on the Harvard Business School study, the Linux Foundation, Tidelift, Black Duck, Oracle, Red Hat and Rimini Street filings, price lists and Homebrew and PyPI analytics, plus earlier positions on open-source.sgit.ai and diniscruz.ai.
